instruction.text: Rachel wants to test the strengths of different magnets. Select a magnet to find out more about her experiment.
Rachel decides she will test the strength of the magnets by seeing how many of an item each magnet can lift. Select which item will work for this experiment.

feedback.correct: That’s right! She can use steel screws for her experiment because they are made out of a magnetic material.
feedback.wrong: Remember, to test the strength of a magnet, the item must be magnetic.

instruction.text: Before doing her experiment, Rachel must make a hypothesis. Select which statement is the better hypothesis.

hint.label: Hypothesis
hint.text: A hypothesis is a prediction about the results of your experiment. The prediction should try to answer the question of your experiment.

feedback.correct: That’s right! This is a good hypothesis because it predicts an answer to the question.
feedback.wrong: Rachel’s hypothesis should try to answer her question of which magnet is the strongest.

b.sound: I think the bar magnet will be the strongest.
I think all the magnets will pick up screws.

instruction.text: Look at Rachel’s experiment below. Is it a fair experiment?

hint.text: A fair experiment should only change one thing at a time. That way, you can be sure that any differences in results are because of that change.
A fair experiment should only change one thing at a time. That way, you can be sure that any differences in results are because of that change.

atoms.b: Rachel’s experiment is not fair because she is using different ((magnets ++screws)).

feedback.wrong: Rachel’s experiment is all about testing different magnets, so it is okay for these to change.

instruction.text: Rachel tests four magnets in total and records her results on this graph. Answer Rachel’s questions about her experiment.

atoms.a: Which magnet was the least powerful?
Which magnet was the most powerful?
How many screws did the bar magnet pick up?
How many <u>more</u> screws did the green magnet pick up than the bar magnet?
